title: Automations: rules from everything you built
tasks: condition(description), describe(), after_dark(), between(start, end), device_is(id, **expected) and payload_is(key, value)
Rule (frozen dataclass) whose evaluate() returns a verdict and a reason; effects light_on, light_off, run and notify
RuleEngine: subscribe to "*", skip rule.* events, evaluate matching rules, isolate failures, keep status and a log, announce rule.fired
Add the bedtime and sunrise routines and six rules named Welcome light, Lights off when empty, Welcome home, Goodnight, Sunrise blinds and Heating notice, plus the automations() hook
explanation: Each rule is plain data: an event name, conditions that only look, and an effect that acts. The conditions and effects come from factories (after_dark(), light_on(60)), the descriptions come from a decorator with arguments, and the clock arrives through the injected context, so the same engine runs against fakes in tests. The engine is just another observer on the bus: it ignores its own announcements, catches failures per rule, and records why each decision was made.

hints.title: Conditions
hints.content: condition(description) returns mark(func) which sets func.description = description and returns func. after_dark builds @condition("it is dark") def check(ctx): return ctx.daylight.is_dark() and returns check. between: if start <= end return start <= now < end, otherwise return now >= start or now < end, using ctx.clock.now().

hints.title: Rule and effects
hints.content: evaluate loops over self.when: if not check(ctx): return False, f"needs: {describe(check)}". At the end return True, " and ".join([f"{self.on} event", *(describe(c) for c in self.when)]). light_on(level, room) returns effect(ctx) which finds ctx.devices.get(f"{room or ctx.event.payload.get('room')}_light") and executes "dim".

hints.title: The engine
hints.content: In _on_event: return early if event.name.startswith("rule."); build a Context; for each rule with rule.on == event.name evaluate it, run rule.then(ctx) inside try/except Exception when it fired, update self.status[rule.name], append to self.log, and emit rule.fired after a real fire. Routines: ROUTINES["bedtime"] = chain(goodnight, blinds_to(0)) and ROUTINES["sunrise"] = blinds_to(100).

checks.prompt: Why must `RuleEngine._on_event` ignore events whose name starts with `rule.`?

options: Those events are slower to process
The engine listens to every event and emits rule.fired itself, so it would react to its own announcements and could loop forever
The scene cannot display them otherwise

checks.explanation: A wildcard subscriber sees everything, including what it publishes. Naming a family of internal events and excluding them is the standard way to avoid a feedback loop.

checks.prompt: The Goodnight rule has a condition "something is still on or unlocked". What problem does it solve?

options: It makes the rule run faster
Time events keep arriving after 23:00, so without a state check the rule would fire again on every one
It prevents the lock from opening
It is only there for the dashboard

checks.explanation: Time-based rules should also check state. The clock stays past 23:00 for hours, but once the house is shut down there is nothing left to do, so the rule skips and says why.

checks.prompt: Which earlier idea does `@condition("it is dark")` rely on?

options: A decorator with arguments (a factory that returns the real decorator)

checks.explanation: `condition(text)` runs first and returns `mark`, which then receives the function: three layers of closures, just like `retry(times=3)`.
